HR-ToF-AMs can indicate organic niterates if they are more than 15 to 60% of the mass of inorganic nitrate in the sample, and that FTIR can identify and quantify functional groups in the sample, but neither HR-ToF-ams nor FTIR uniquely identifies specific organic nitrated species.
FTIR spectroscopy can be applied to particles to determine the functional group composition and that the HR-ToF-AMs can be applied to detect the presence of organic nitrates in particles.

HR-ToF-AMs can be used to determine the relative abundance of organic nitrates, but cannot be used for identification of specific organic nitrate species, and that FTIR is the preferred method for identification and quantification.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods to detect organic nitrates and to identify their structures.
the measurement of organic nitrates in atmospheric aerosols.
the development of a new method for the measurement of organic nitrates, which are formed during the oxidation of volatile organic carbon (VOC) species in the atmosphere.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NO(+)/NO2(+) ratio from HRToF-AMS is not sufficient to identify the presence of organic nitrate, but it is a necessary condition for the presence of organic nitrates in the aerosol.

HR-ToF- AMS is not a good tool for the identification and quantification, and FTIR spectroscopic analysis of organic nitrates in particles is a good tool for their identification but is not quantitative.
HR-ToF-AM and FTIR spectroscopies are complementary methods for characterizing organic nitrates in atmospheric aerosol.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
FTIR spectroscopy and HR-ToF-AM are complementary techniques for identifying organic nitrates in particles.

FTIR is more useful than HR-ToF-AMs for the detection of organic nitrates, but that both techniques are useful for the detection of multifunctional organic compounds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HR-ToF-AMs and FTIR spectroscopic methods are complementary and that the combination of both methods can provide a powerful approach to the study of organic nitrates in the atmosphere.
FTIR spectroscopy is a useful technique for the identification and quantification (relative to inorganic nitrates) of organic nitrate groups in particles.

the NO(+) and NO(2)(+) ions from HR-ToF and SPLAT II mass spectrometers are not specific for organic nitrates, and that the N/H ratios from these instruments are not reliable indicators of the amount of organic nitrate in a sample, unless the amount of organic nitrates greatly exceeds that of inorganic nitrates.
